text: By the early 1800s, the company's private army in India was about 200,000 strong, bigger
than the British army itself.
Its rise began with a bored young clerk in Madras who found out he was much better at
war than at paperwork, Robert Clive.
In 1757, at Plassie in Bengal, Clive's small army faced the Nawab of Bengal.
But Clive had already made a secret deal with the Nawab's own commander.
When the battle began, much of the Nawab's army simply stood still.
One of the most important battles in Indian history was won by a deal.
Within a few years, the company won the right to collect the taxes of Bengal, one of the
richest provinces on earth.
A company now ruled millions of people, and its first priority was profit.
In 1770, a terrible famine struck Bengal.
Some estimates say up to a third of the population died.
The company didn't cut its taxes, it raised them.
In these same years, English picked up a new word from India, lut.
From the Hindi lut, plunder.
Not everyone gave in.
Tipu Sultan of Mysore fought the company with iron cased rockets so good that the British
copied them.
In the Punjab, Ranjit Singh built a Sikh empire that kept the company out for 40 years.
He even got the coenour.
But after he died, the company took the Punjab, and the diamond went to Queen Victoria.
Remember our question?
Every robber before had stayed and become part of India.
This one kept its headquarters in London.
By the 1850s, the company controlled most of India, and the soldiers it relied on most,
the seapoys, were Indian.
That was about to matter, a lot.
